One day you may be walking along a seashore. You glance back to watch your footprints disappear with the next surge of foaming water. You love to hear the soothing swish of the breakers. You gaze at the graceful sweep of shoreline and glittering ocean way out to the horizon. Life is good.

Suddenly a huge wave sweeps in and lifts you off your feet. You struggle and flail to regain your footing. Or the wave may even carry you farther and slam you against a rock wall, leaving you stunned and gasping in pain.

This wave may be called grief, as expressed in the following stanza from the song by Mary A. Baker.

Master, with anguish of spirit
I bow in my grief today;
The depths of my sad heart are troubled;
Oh, waken and save, I pray!
Torrents of sin and of anguish
Sweep o’er my sinking soul!
And I perish! I perish, dear Master;
Oh hasten, and take control.

In the past year, many of us have lost loved ones. Perhaps it was a childhood friend, or someone from our church family, or even from our immediate family. Depending on how close we were, we felt drops, splashes, or even tidal waves of grief.

Our grief stems from the relationship we shared. We have invested in each other’s lives to some degree. We have loved, but now that love has nowhere to go. We could say that grief is the price of love.

Here is how one widow described grief: “At the sudden and untimely death of my husband, the feeling was one of overwhelming shock, disbelief, and even panic, as I faced an uncertain future without him at the age of 51. Looking back, I realize how merciful God is to allow us to be in a certain state of numbness and shock at a time like this, allowing the reality to sink in more slowly.”

How did she cope? She says, “I am also awed at how He provides the grace and strength to go through hard things in life that we never thought we would have to face. He walks with us as we go through the valley of grief, so we are never walking alone. The journey of grief is not the same for everyone. It is not over in a few months. For me, I still cried a year later. It took a long time for the pain to fade and for life to become meaningful again. But praise God, that time does come! It is best not to look too far into the future. We walk one day at a time with Jesus, knowing that the best is yet to come.”

Here are more experiences from those who have been there:

  • “I am still learning that when we say, ‘It’s all right, Lord,’ we need to leave it there, at Jesus’ feet.”
  • “Grieving people are very lonely, but there’s also an aloneness that comes from not having a place to belong. You may be in a room of people, and still feel utterly alone, because you’ve lost your sense of belonging, or your category of belonging has changed.”
  • “The presence of a grieving person can be painful for others. It’s a reminder that “bad” things can happen. So, at times they are not invited, which is painful. A grieving person wants to be invited, but at times when included they feel their lack of belonging anew and think they should have stayed at home. Most times, casual conversation can be difficult for them when their world has been violently shaken. Their hearts are heavy while the mood of others is lighthearted, making them feel even more despondent. Understandably, many people don’t know what to do when they see others grieving, so they default to doing nothing and walk away. Many friendships are lost after a loss, which is even more painful.”
  • “God was so close. He was always there. ‘Underneath are the everlasting arms’, and I felt them.”

God can use sorrow and grief to teach us what we might not learn in happier times. We learn to depend on Him. We think of the seriousness of life. We learn to embrace eternal values and anticipate heaven. We are motivated to cherish the loved ones we still have when we hear expressions such as this: “Looking back, I wish we would not have taken the time we had together for granted. I wish I would have recognized his personality traits as strengths rather than things that annoyed.”

Those who lose loved ones often find themselves in the limelight for a time. Many people want to know how they are responding, especially when the death is an unusual situation. Consider the experience of Elizabeth Elliot and the four others who were made widows in 1956 by jungle killers in Ecuador. Or think of Marie Troyer whose husband John was murdered by guerrillas in Guatemala in 1981, or the mothers of the girls killed in Nickel Mines, Pennsylvania in 2006.

These women found themselves in the glare of an almost worldwide spotlight. Their greatest opportunity to display God’s enabling grace likely came at a time when they wanted it least. But their responses of forgiveness, unselfishness, and trust in God amazed the world, at least considering the amount of media attention. Truly, A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid –Matthew 5:14.

While we and those we know will hardly face that level of exposure, we too have a unique platform to display God’s grace. We may never have a better opportunity to touch hardened or seeking hearts than in our own hour of grief.

When we hear that people have indeed been drawn to God through the death of our loved one, it can be a source of comfort and meaning. This death was not a senseless tragedy; it was meant to bring glory to God. In other words, God does not waste our sorrows.

It reminds us of Jesus’ words about Lazarus when he said, …This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God might be glorified thereby –John 11:4. Jesus is our perfect example for relating to those in sorrow. He came to Mary and Martha and listened. He cried with them even though He knew He could and then did transform the whole situation by raising Lazarus.

How do we help?

What is our part in helping a grieving sister glorify God in the midst of her situation? Consider the thoughts shared by the following widows:

  • “What helped was when a dear sister sat with me and told me she cared. And in her quietness, I could feel that her love was real.”
  • “Grief is surprising and unexpected. The person may be having a good day when they hear a song, smell a certain scent, or see a familiar article of clothing which triggers a memory followed by a flood of tears. If this happens when you’re with them, it’s okay. Tears are okay. Tears are healing. Stay present and help them through it. Press in; grieve with them. It’s better to err in doing something than in doing nothing. You may not understand. That’s okay. You don’t need to experience loss to show that you care.”
  • “Grief is exhausting and mentally debilitating. So don’t just ask what you can do; look for a need they may have and try to fill it. For example, ‘I’d like to come over Tuesday evening and fix your faucet’ or ‘We’d like to come and bring a meal if you’re up to it?’”
  • “One thing that meant a lot to me was when people shared pleasant memories of our loved one, or things they appreciated about him. Even today, almost nineteen years later, it still warms my heart when people do that.”
  • “It was all the cards that came every day for the first two months after my husband died. I looked forward to them every day, and the first day without a card was hard.”
  • “What really helped me was when someone told me to focus on my blessings; that they are praying for me, and they care. Or they invited me to go along even if the number was then lopsided. Another thing was when they stopped by for coffee breaks or when they sent a text.”
  • “Widows need encouragement on their anniversary date and on the date their husband died. It means a lot if someone ‘actually’ remembers! A widow’s supper is nice. So is having a secret sister. It helped when someone gave a listening ear and was there to help with the work and the young children. Most of all, I knew people were praying for us.”

What do we say?

We may struggle with what to say to a bereaved friend. After all, we do not want to be like Job’s wife or his friends whose words only increased Job’s suffering. Here are some perspectives:

  • “They need not tell us we are alone now. We know that already.”
  • “Grief may really shake someone’s faith in God, momentarily paralyzing them, especially if they haven’t experienced much trauma before. As much as they long to trust God and accept this new reality in their lives, sometimes it takes time to simply get through the shock and be able to talk to God again. This is okay. They will most likely find healing and deepen their faith, but give them space to struggle, wrestle, and grieve deeply. Listen and try to refrain from “fixing” their faith with words such as “All things work together for good…”, or “At least you…”
  • “Asking a grieving person how they are doing could put them in a difficult position. Asking in a crowd of people may not be the best time. It may be best not to ask unless you really want to know and are willing to take the time to listen.”
  • “It is hard to think rationally in those first hard months. I did not appreciate being asked those first months what I would do for a living. I first needed to process my grief. I was also trying to help my young daughters who were devastated at the loss of their beloved daddy. That decision could wait.”

The following excerpts reveal other struggles with grief:

  • “Everyone grieves differently; there is no right or wrong way. And it never goes away even though all my friends’ lives go on as normal, which is very painful to watch. Holidays are very hard. Attending weddings is almost not doable. This is a couple’s world and only by the grace of God is it possible. Actually, the weeks before the annual anniversary dates are harder than the actual days.”
  • “One thing I realized very quickly was that we live in a very couple-orientated world. At the loss of a spouse, one is left trying to figure out where they fit in. I deeply appreciate, when I’m in a group setting that includes widows and singles, that there are those who try to make me feel included and not the odd one out.”
  • “You can’t put a time limit on grief. It’s different for everyone. There’s no ‘getting over it’ so that it doesn’t hurt anymore. If grieved properly, the wound is not as raw, and it becomes a scar. It’s like getting used to living without an arm or a leg. You adjust to it not being there, but you never stop missing it.”
  • “Death in the family or losing a spouse is harder than one can imagine until they are going through the same thing. I wish we would have had more church support. Our boys need a father figure to follow, one to teach them what a dad would.”
  • “Our children make mistakes as other children do; they need encouragement, not criticism. Also, they could use a helping hand with their work. I wish I would not have needed to leave my youngest child alone so much when I went to work. I broke out in a sweat more than once wondering where the money was coming from to pay the bills, but I thank the Lord that it was always there.”

How can we remember to support the grieving beyond those first days and weeks? We could mark our calendars with the dates of their birthdays, anniversaries, and their loved one’s death date. Then we could designate a certain day of the week to do something for them. If we make a plan, we are more likely to carry out our good intentions.

Finally, we should also remember the “widows who aren’t”. Sometimes there are those among us whose life is racked by a grief worse than that of an actual death. Perhaps there was betrayal, abandonment, incarceration, or suicide in their life’s journey. They may almost envy the clean wound of the “normal” widow. Or they may struggle with guilt on top of their grief.

These situations are often located far outside our comfort zones. There are no easy answers of how to deal with them. But let us not stay aloof from such a sister if we have the opportunity. God will help us find a way to show we care if we ask Him.

As we, and those we love, keep walking with God, may we portray the scene in the final verse of the song mentioned earlier:

“Master, the terror is over, the elements sweetly rest;
Earth’s sun in the calm lake is mirrored,
And heaven’s within my breast.
Linger, O blessed Redeemer,
Leave me alone no more;
And with joy I shall make the blest harbor,
And rest on the blissful shore.”

Let’s conclude with a quote from a widow:

“Walk with them until they can come out of the cave and feel the sunshine again. It may require hard work and getting messy at times, but to them you will be Jesus ‘with skin on’. You are not responsible for their healing; only Jesus can do that. But you can bring them to Him.

Remember the friends that brought the paralyzed man to Jesus, lowering him through the roof. And, behold, they brought to him a man sick of the palsy, lying on a bed: and Jesus seeing their faith said unto the sick of the palsy; Son, be of good cheer; thy sins be forgiven thee … And Jesus knowing their thoughts said, Wherefore think ye evil in your hearts? For whether is easier, to say, Thy sins be forgiven thee; or to say, Arise, and walk? But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power on earth to forgive sins, (then saith he to the sick of the palsy,) Arise, take up thy bed, and go unto thine house. And he arose, and departed to his house. But when the multitudes saw it, they marvelled, and glorified God, which had given such power unto men –Matthew 9:2-8.

What a beautiful picture! In like manner, you can carry your grief-‘paralyzed’ friend to Jesus. Watch them be healed, shoulder their burden of grief, and then move on toward their heavenly home. As we see God doing a work in their heart, we can all praise God together!”

~In this article, the sections in quotation marks were shared with the author by a number of anonymous widows.

","section":"SISTER TO SISTER","subtitle":null,"title":"To Walk With Her Through Grief"},"source_context":{"byline":{"authors":[{"location":"Lakeville, OH","name":"Naomi Lapp"}],"raw":"by Naomi Lapp Lakeville, OH"}},"target_language":"French","terminology_glossary":{},"translation":{"html":"

Un jour, vous vous promenez peut-être le long du rivage. Vous vous retournez pour regarder vos empreintes disparaître sous la prochaine vague d’eau écumante. Vous aimez entendre le doux bruissement des vagues qui déferlent. Vous contemplez la courbe gracieuse du littoral et l’océan scintillant qui s’étend jusqu’à l’horizon. La vie est belle.

Soudain, une immense vague déferle et vous soulève. Vous luttez et battez des bras pour retrouver votre équilibre. Ou bien la vague vous emporte plus loin et vous projette contre une paroi rocheuse, vous laissant étourdi et haletant de douleur.

Cette vague pourrait s’appeler le chagrin, comme l’exprime la strophe suivante du chant de Mary A. Baker.

Maître, le cœur plein d’angoisse,
Je m’incline aujourd’hui dans mon chagrin ;
Les profondeurs de mon cœur affligé sont troublées ;
Oh, éveille-toi et sauve-moi, je t’en prie !
Les torrents du péché et de l’angoisse
Submergent mon âme qui sombre !
Et je péris ! Je péris, cher Maître ;
Oh, hâte-toi et prends les choses en main.

Au cours de l’année écoulée, beaucoup d’entre nous ont perdu des êtres chers. Il s’agissait peut-être d’un ami d’enfance, d’un membre de notre famille d’Église, ou même de notre famille proche. Selon la proximité de notre relation, nous avons ressenti quelques gouttes, des éclaboussures ou même des raz-de-marée de chagrin.

Notre chagrin découle de la relation que nous avions. Nous avons investi l’un dans la vie de l’autre, à des degrés divers. Nous avons aimé, mais maintenant cet amour n’a plus où se porter. On pourrait dire que le chagrin est le prix de l’amour.

Voici comment une veuve a décrit le chagrin : « À la mort soudaine et prématurée de mon mari, j’ai été submergée par le choc, l’incrédulité et même la panique, face à un avenir incertain sans lui, à l’âge de 51 ans. Avec le recul, je comprends combien Dieu est miséricordieux de nous laisser dans un certain état d’engourdissement et de choc à un moment pareil, et de permettre ainsi à la réalité de s’imposer plus lentement. »

Comment a-t-elle fait face ? Elle dit : « Je suis aussi émerveillée de voir comment Il donne la grâce et la force de traverser les épreuves de la vie que nous n’aurions jamais cru devoir affronter. Il marche avec nous dans la vallée du chagrin, si bien que nous ne marchons jamais seuls. Le chemin du deuil n’est pas le même pour tous. Il ne se termine pas en quelques mois. Pour moi, je pleurais encore un an plus tard. Il a fallu beaucoup de temps pour que la douleur s’atténue et que la vie retrouve un sens. Mais, loué soit Dieu, ce moment finit par arriver ! Mieux vaut ne pas regarder trop loin dans l’avenir. Nous avançons un jour à la fois avec Jésus, sachant que le meilleur est encore à venir. »

Voici d’autres témoignages de personnes qui sont passées par là :

  • « J’apprends encore que lorsque nous disons : “C’est bien, Seigneur”, nous devons nous en tenir là, aux pieds de Jésus. »
  • « Les personnes endeuillées se sentent très seules, mais il y a aussi une solitude qui vient du fait de ne pas avoir de place à laquelle appartenir. On peut être dans une pièce remplie de monde et se sentir tout de même complètement seul, parce qu’on a perdu le sentiment d’appartenir à un groupe, ou que sa place au sein de ce groupe a changé. »
  • « La présence d’une personne en deuil peut être douloureuse pour les autres. Elle leur rappelle que de “mauvaises” choses peuvent arriver. Alors, parfois, on ne l’invite pas, ce qui est douloureux. Une personne endeuillée souhaite être invitée, mais lorsqu’elle est incluse, il lui arrive de ressentir à nouveau qu’elle n’a pas sa place et de penser qu’elle aurait dû rester chez elle. La plupart du temps, les conversations légères peuvent lui être difficiles, alors que son monde a été violemment bouleversé. Son cœur est lourd tandis que les autres sont d’humeur insouciante, ce qui la rend encore plus accablée. Il est compréhensible que beaucoup ne sachent pas quoi faire lorsqu’ils voient quelqu’un en deuil ; ils finissent donc par ne rien faire et s’éloignent. Après un deuil, beaucoup d’amitiés se perdent, ce qui est encore plus douloureux. »
  • « Dieu était si proche. Il était toujours là. “Les bras éternels sont au-dessous”, et je les ai sentis. »

Dieu peut se servir de la tristesse et du chagrin pour nous enseigner ce que nous n’apprendrions peut-être pas dans les périodes plus heureuses. Nous apprenons à dépendre de Lui. Nous réfléchissons au sérieux de la vie. Nous apprenons à embrasser les valeurs éternelles et à attendre le ciel. Nous sommes poussés à chérir les êtres chers qui nous restent lorsque nous entendons des paroles comme celles-ci : « Avec le recul, j’aurais aimé ne pas avoir considéré comme acquis le temps que nous avons passé ensemble. J’aurais aimé reconnaître les traits de sa personnalité comme des qualités plutôt que comme des choses qui m’agaçaient. »

Ceux qui perdent des êtres chers se retrouvent souvent sous les feux des projecteurs pendant un certain temps. Beaucoup veulent savoir comment ils réagissent, surtout lorsque la mort survient dans des circonstances inhabituelles. Pensons à l’expérience d’Elizabeth Elliot et des quatre autres femmes devenues veuves en 1956 après que des tueurs dans la jungle équatorienne ont assassiné leurs maris. Ou à Marie Troyer, dont le mari John a été assassiné par des guérilleros au Guatemala en 1981, ou encore aux mères des filles tuées à Nickel Mines, en Pennsylvanie, en 2006.

Ces femmes se sont retrouvées sous les projecteurs d’une attention presque mondiale. C’est probablement au moment où elles le désiraient le moins qu’elles ont eu la plus grande occasion de manifester la grâce de Dieu qui les rend capables. Mais leurs réactions — le pardon, le désintéressement et la confiance en Dieu — ont émerveillé le monde, du moins compte tenu de l’ampleur de l’attention médiatique. En vérité, Une ville située sur une montagne ne peut être cachée –Matthieu 5:14.

Nous et ceux que nous connaissons ne serons probablement jamais exposés à ce point, mais nous avons, nous aussi, une occasion unique de manifester la grâce de Dieu. Nous n’aurons peut-être jamais de meilleure occasion de toucher des cœurs endurcis ou en quête de Dieu que dans notre propre heure de chagrin.

Apprendre que des personnes ont effectivement été attirées vers Dieu par la mort de notre être cher peut être une source de réconfort et de sens. Cette mort n’était pas une tragédie insensée ; elle devait servir à la gloire de Dieu. Autrement dit, Dieu ne gaspille pas nos chagrins.

Cela nous rappelle les paroles de Jésus au sujet de Lazare : …Cette maladie n’est pas pour la mort, mais pour la gloire de Dieu, afin que le Fils de Dieu soit glorifié par elle –Jean 11:4. Jésus est notre parfait exemple dans la manière de nous comporter envers ceux qui sont dans la tristesse. Il est venu auprès de Marie et de Marthe et les a écoutées. Il a pleuré avec elles, bien qu’Il sût qu’Il pouvait, puis a effectivement transformé toute la situation en ressuscitant Lazare.

Comment pouvons-nous aider ?

Quel est notre rôle pour aider une sœur endeuillée à glorifier Dieu au milieu de sa situation ? Réfléchissons aux pensées exprimées par les veuves suivantes :

  • « Ce qui m’a aidée, c’est qu’une chère sœur s’est assise avec moi et m’a dit qu’elle se souciait de moi. Et dans son silence, je pouvais sentir que son amour était sincère. »
  • « Le chagrin est surprenant et inattendu. La personne peut passer une bonne journée, puis entendre une chanson, sentir une odeur particulière ou voir un vêtement familier, ce qui fait resurgir un souvenir, suivi d’un torrent de larmes. Si cela arrive quand vous êtes avec elle, ce n’est pas grave. Les larmes sont normales. Elles font du bien. Restez auprès d’elle et aidez-la à traverser ce moment. Soyez présent ; pleurez avec elle. Mieux vaut risquer d’en faire trop que de ne rien faire. Vous ne comprendrez peut-être pas. Ce n’est pas grave. Vous n’avez pas besoin d’avoir vécu une perte pour montrer que vous vous souciez d’elle. »
  • « Le chagrin est épuisant et affaiblit les facultés mentales. Alors, ne demandez pas seulement ce que vous pouvez faire ; cherchez plutôt un besoin qu’elle pourrait avoir et essayez d’y répondre. Par exemple : “J’aimerais passer mardi soir pour réparer votre robinet” ou “Nous aimerions venir apporter un repas, si vous vous en sentez capable.” »
  • « Une chose qui m’a beaucoup touchée, c’est lorsque des gens partageaient de bons souvenirs de notre être cher, ou des choses qu’ils appréciaient chez lui. Même aujourd’hui, presque dix-neuf ans plus tard, cela me réchauffe toujours le cœur. »
  • « Ce sont toutes les cartes qui arrivaient chaque jour pendant les deux premiers mois après la mort de mon mari. Je les attendais chaque jour, et le premier jour sans carte a été difficile. »
  • « Ce qui m’a vraiment aidée, c’est quand quelqu’un m’a dit de me concentrer sur mes bénédictions, qu’il priait pour moi et qu’il se souciait de moi. Ou quand on m’invitait à me joindre aux autres, même si cela déséquilibrait alors le nombre de personnes. Une autre chose qui m’a fait du bien, c’est lorsque des gens passaient prendre un café ou m’envoyaient un texto. »
  • « Les veuves ont besoin d’encouragement à la date de leur anniversaire de mariage et à la date du décès de leur mari. Cela compte beaucoup quand quelqu’un s’en souvient “vraiment” ! Un repas entre veuves, c’est agréable. Avoir une sœur amie secrète, aussi. Cela m’a aidée quand quelqu’un m’a écoutée et était là pour m’aider dans les tâches et avec les jeunes enfants. Surtout, je savais que des gens priaient pour nous. »

Que dire ?

Nous avons parfois du mal à savoir quoi dire à un ami endeuillé. Après tout, nous ne voulons pas ressembler à la femme de Job ou à ses amis, dont les paroles n’ont fait qu’accroître les souffrances de Job. Voici quelques points de vue :

  • « Ils n’ont pas besoin de nous dire que nous sommes seuls désormais. Nous le savons déjà. »
  • « Le chagrin peut vraiment ébranler la foi de quelqu’un en Dieu et le paralyser momentanément, surtout s’il n’a pas connu beaucoup de traumatismes auparavant. Même s’il aspire à faire confiance à Dieu et à accepter cette nouvelle réalité dans sa vie, il lui faut parfois du temps simplement pour sortir du choc et être capable de parler de nouveau à Dieu. Ce n’est pas grave. Il finira probablement par guérir et sa foi s’approfondira, mais laissez-lui l’espace nécessaire pour lutter, se débattre et vivre profondément son deuil. Écoutez-le et essayez de ne pas “réparer” sa foi avec des paroles comme : “Toutes choses concourent au bien…” ou “Au moins, tu…” »
  • « Demander à une personne endeuillée comment elle va peut la mettre dans une situation difficile. Le lui demander au milieu d’un groupe n’est peut-être pas le meilleur moment. Mieux vaut peut-être ne pas poser la question, à moins de vouloir vraiment savoir et d’être prêt à prendre le temps de l’écouter. »
  • « Il est difficile de penser rationnellement pendant ces premiers mois éprouvants. Je n’ai pas apprécié qu’on me demande, au cours de ces premiers mois, ce que j’allais faire comme travail. Je devais d’abord vivre mon deuil. J’essayais aussi d’aider mes jeunes filles, dévastées par la perte de leur papa bien-aimé. Cette décision pouvait attendre. »

Les extraits suivants révèlent d’autres difficultés liées au deuil :

  • « Chacun vit son deuil différemment ; il n’y a pas de bonne ou de mauvaise manière de le vivre. Et il ne disparaît jamais, même si la vie de tous mes amis continue normalement, ce qui est très douloureux à voir. Les fêtes sont très difficiles. Assister à des mariages est presque impossible. C’est un monde fait pour les couples, et seule la grâce de Dieu rend cela possible. En fait, les semaines précédant les dates anniversaires sont plus difficiles que les jours mêmes. »
  • « J’ai très vite compris que nous vivons dans un monde très centré sur les couples. Lorsqu’on perd son conjoint, on se retrouve à essayer de comprendre quelle est sa place. J’apprécie profondément, lorsque je suis dans un groupe où se trouvent des veuves et des célibataires, que certaines personnes s’efforcent de me faire sentir incluse et de ne pas me laisser à part. »
  • « On ne peut pas fixer de limite de temps au chagrin. C’est différent pour chacun. On ne “s’en remet” pas au point que cela ne fasse plus mal. Si le deuil est bien vécu, la blessure est moins à vif et devient une cicatrice. C’est comme apprendre à vivre sans un bras ou une jambe. On s’adapte à leur absence, mais ils nous manquent toujours. »
  • « La mort d’un membre de la famille ou la perte d’un conjoint est plus difficile qu’on ne peut l’imaginer tant qu’on ne traverse pas soi-même la même épreuve. J’aurais aimé que nous ayons davantage de soutien de l’Église. Nos garçons ont besoin d’une figure paternelle à suivre, de quelqu’un qui leur enseigne ce qu’un père enseignerait. »
  • « Nos enfants font des erreurs comme les autres enfants ; ils ont besoin d’encouragement, pas de critiques. Ils auraient aussi besoin d’un coup de main pour leurs tâches. J’aurais aimé ne pas avoir à laisser si souvent mon plus jeune enfant seul quand j’allais travailler. Plus d’une fois, j’ai eu des sueurs froides en me demandant d’où viendrait l’argent pour payer les factures, mais je remercie le Seigneur, car il y en a toujours eu. »

Comment pouvons-nous penser à soutenir les personnes endeuillées au-delà des premiers jours et des premières semaines ? Nous pourrions noter dans nos calendriers les dates de leurs anniversaires, de leurs anniversaires de mariage et du décès de leur être cher. Puis nous pourrions choisir un jour précis de la semaine pour faire quelque chose pour elles. Si nous établissons un plan, nous sommes plus susceptibles de concrétiser nos bonnes intentions.

Enfin, nous devrions aussi nous souvenir des « veuves qui n’en sont pas ». Il y a parfois parmi nous des personnes dont la vie est ravagée par un chagrin plus douloureux que celui causé par une mort réelle. Peut-être ont-elles connu la trahison, l’abandon, l’incarcération ou le suicide au cours de leur vie. Elles peuvent presque envier la blessure nette de la veuve « ordinaire ». Ou bien elles peuvent lutter contre la culpabilité en plus de leur chagrin.

Ces situations se trouvent souvent bien au-delà de notre zone de confort. Il n’existe pas de réponse facile à la question de savoir comment y faire face. Mais ne restons pas à l’écart d’une telle sœur si nous en avons l’occasion. Dieu nous aidera à trouver une façon de lui montrer que nous nous soucions d’elle, si nous le Lui demandons.

Alors que nous-mêmes et ceux que nous aimons continuons à marcher avec Dieu, puissions-nous représenter la scène du dernier vers du chant mentionné plus tôt :

« Maître, la tempête est passée, les éléments reposent en paix ;
Le soleil terrestre se reflète dans le lac calme,
Et le ciel est dans mon cœur.
Demeure, ô bienheureux Rédempteur,
Ne me laisse plus seul ;
Et c’est avec joie que j’atteindrai le port béni,
Et me reposerai sur le rivage bienheureux. »

Concluons par les paroles d’une veuve :

« Marchez avec eux jusqu’à ce qu’ils puissent sortir de la grotte et sentir à nouveau la chaleur du soleil. Cela peut demander beaucoup d’efforts et parfois vous mettre dans des situations difficiles, mais pour eux, vous serez Jésus “en chair et en os”. Vous n’êtes pas responsable de leur guérison ; seul Jésus peut l’accomplir. Mais vous pouvez les conduire à Lui.

Souvenez-vous des amis qui ont amené le paralytique à Jésus en le descendant par le toit. Et voici, on lui amena un paralytique couché sur un lit ; Jésus, voyant leur foi, dit au paralytique : Mon fils, prends courage, tes péchés te sont pardonnés… Jésus, connaissant leurs pensées, dit : Pourquoi avez-vous de mauvaises pensées dans vos cœurs ? Qu’est-ce qui est le plus facile, de dire : Tes péchés te sont pardonnés, ou de dire : Lève-toi et marche ? Mais afin que vous sachiez que le Fils de l’homme a sur la terre le pouvoir de pardonner les péchés, il dit alors au paralytique : Lève-toi, prends ton lit et va dans ta maison. Et il se leva et s’en alla dans sa maison. Quand les foules virent cela, elles furent saisies d’admiration et glorifièrent Dieu, qui a donné un tel pouvoir aux hommes –Matthieu 9:2-8.

Quelle belle image ! De la même manière, vous pouvez porter à Jésus votre ami “paralysé” par le chagrin. Regardez-le guérir, porter le fardeau de son chagrin, puis avancer vers sa demeure céleste. Lorsque nous voyons Dieu agir dans son cœur, nous pouvons tous louer Dieu ensemble ! »

~Dans cet article, les passages entre guillemets ont été communiqués à l’auteure par plusieurs veuves anonymes.

And David said, What have I now done? Is there not a cause? –1 Samuel 17:29.

The story of David and Goliath took place over three millenniums ago and has been a perennial favorite of the young and old ever since. There is something about the plight of the underdog that we all relate to. Perhaps we subconsciously view ourselves in such odds and secretly hope that there will come a day when our own “ship will come in” in a similar fashion. Unfortunately, that sort of random success seems more akin to a Hollywood production than to real life. We see only the conflict between the young and the old, the shepherd and the warrior, and the heavy military weapons and the sling. Yet there were some preliminary principles that David embraced in his youth that made him a prime candidate for success. But these often go unheralded in our love for a climactic romantic victory.

If the only vision we have of ourselves comes from the social mirror about us, we will carry a warped inner perception similar to what we see as we glance into a trick mirror at a carnival. The social opinions and perceptions of our environment often cast an awkward and skewed description of our person before our eyes and ears. Sometimes it is unrealistically positive, building the person up in the eyes of the media when there is very little heroic character displayed.

The sports arena is probably the biggest offender in this. The individuals are praised who can run, throw, or shoot better than everyone else. But sporting talent adds little to their honest pure worth as a human. The other side of the coin produces an immense amount of negative and degrading input that seeks to thwart any effort to try. These comments are produced in copious showers by stressed parents, insecure siblings, frustrated bosses, and a host of other acquaintances struggling for identity in a “survival of the fittest” society. The input from these two camps is both disjointed, and out of proportion. To be told you are great will never produce greatness any more than a barrage of derogatory remarks will produce humility. Unfortunately, too often many of us allow these disproportionate projections to affect our thinking and chart our course.

The greatest and superior endowment given to mankind over the rest of creation is not found in his physical abilities, but in his mind. The most intelligent of animals can be trained to be responsible, but they cannot choose or direct that training. But as humans, we can write new programs for ourselves totally independent of our instincts or environmental training. Those of us who live in natural accordance with our instincts and conditioning, will scarcely rise above the animal kingdom. But those who will exercise and develop those endowments shall uniquely fill the role God has designed for them in their encounter with the giants. While David’s time and position were unique, the principles he embraced were universal. If I could teach my dog to yodel, it would prove that yodeling is achievable for dogs and open the possibility for others to do it too. Likewise, if David defeated Goliath by miracle alone, then there is no hope for us but to sit and wait for God to do the same for us. However, if principles were at the core of the victory, then there is an example for us to follow and a virtue to secure for use on our own battlefield.

As David arose early that morning and shouldered his pack of corn, bread, and cheese to take to his brothers, he had no idea what the day would bring forth. The Lord was his Shepherd, and he had no lack, but as he came upon the scene he was shocked at the sight. Both armies were positioned on opposite mountains and locked in a stalemate. To take your entire army down into the valley and fight the opposition uphill would leave you at a tremendous disadvantage. One that neither side was willing to risk. So, the Philistines evoked a common dimension of warfare proposing that two warriors would fight in the valley giving no advantage to either side. But the Philistines had a giant among their numbers that terrified the army of Israel. As David inquired into the situation as to why no one would confront the reproachful blasphemies of the infidel, he was met with a stiff rebuke from his oldest brother: …and Eliab’s anger was kindled against David, and he said, Why camest thou down hither? and with whom hast thou left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart; for thou art come down that thou mightest see the battle. And David said, What have I now done? Is there not a cause? –1 Samuel 17:28-29.

Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God –Hebrews 12:2. When a man has a cause set before him, he can endure almost anything. Some endure for a corruptible crown. King Saul had offered tax exempt wealth and son-in-law status, but the earthly dowry elicited no volunteers. While the thought of earthly prominence meant nothing to the tender heart of David, there was a jealous fire kindled by the blasphemous taunts of Goliath and he stepped forward by faith. But faith is not just a whim that may be inflated by an emotional tire pump. For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works [action] is dead also –James 2:26. Thus, with the cause clearly before him, and his God beside him, David offers to fight Goliath.

So David moved forward acting according to godly, uncorrupted principles…

A Caring Conscience is seated in the soul of man and determines what we care about. Many think that a conscience is only useful as a limiting guide. But the human conscience was also created to function in the reverse. When we are convicted that something is good and right, we pursue it with a passion. Thomas Edison said that genius is 1% inspiration and 99% perspiration. While this may be true enough, it is without question that the inspiration must arrive first. Jacob’s aspirations for Rachael made him forget the seven years of labor. Edison’s pursuit of a successful light bulb caused him to forget the thousands of elements that had failed.

Careless apathy is the opposite and is the result of a seared conscience. David was amazed that the blasphemous taunts of Goliath produced no cause for action on the part of God’s army. Give a man a reason to live and he will supply the how –Nietzke. As a holocaust prisoner in a Nazi concentration camp, Victor Frankl was commissioned to labor in the ward of the camp where prisoners were dying of typhus. He observed that when a person gave up hope, death was soon to follow. Likewise, for many of our day, when the hope of personal gain evaporates in the fray, so does the passion to overcome. Most workers today are more concerned about their paycheck than of doing a good and worthy job. Often when a man loses his feelings for his wife, he believes that he is incapable of loving her, but a man with a healthy conscience toward godly principles will act in loving fashion toward her regardless of his feelings or her response. The cause is aroused and fueled by the conscience and lays the foundation for passionate action.

An Honest Imagination belongs to the realm of the spirit and is driven by our conscience. Necessity is the mother of invention –Unknown. Some are waiting for life to be discovered while others are inventing it as they go. This is not a license to claim false ideals. David’s pursuit is honest for he was not warped by the media about him. He has met with success over the beasts (a lion and a bear) in the hills of Bethlehem and with God’s help, incurs no fear of contending with one (a man of war from his youth) in the valley of Elah.

As Saul reluctantly consents to David’s proposal, he proceeds to arm the lad in typical worldly fashion. While it may have been an honor to wear the armor of the king, David would have none of it: …I cannot go with these; for I have not proved them. And David put them off him –1 Samuel 17:39, choosing five stones instead. Knowing what others do and knowing what to do are not necessarily the same thing.

The cowering beliefs of the Israelite army were rooted in a pagan value system. Goliath was not the problem, but rather, faithless fear and the assumption that they needed to engage in the warfare on the terms of the world. Those that embrace a true and worthy cause will surely find the imagination to pursue it.

Goliath had automatically assumed that he would be in combat under his own terms. Insulted and angered he cries out: …Come to me, and I will give thy flesh unto the fowls of the air, and to the beasts of the field –1 Samuel 17:44. As a giant, speed and agility are not his forte and so he orders David to come to him. But Goliath has grossly overestimated his personal ability and underestimated his foe. According to some estimates, at six or seven revolutions per second, David’s sling had the stopping power of a 45 mm handgun, and the hand of a skillful slinger …could sling stones at an hair breadth, and not miss –Judges 20:16. It was not unusual for them to be able to hit birds in flight. Ancient ruins have uncovered tongs that were believed to be used by the military to remove embedded stones from wounded soldiers. If Goliath had a spear and David a pistol, we would not be so quick to believe that the larger man held the major advantage.

Faithful Action is inevitable when our bodies are subject to our soul and spirit, and they are under the direction of God’s Spirit. We are then free to act independently of our nature and other influences. When the lustful passions of the mortal body hold sway over our inner heart and mind, we are defeated before we take one step toward the enemy. As vessels of God’s design, with a moral free will, we have the divine ability to choose our course of action. Some believe that being proactive is merely taking the initiative. But initiative alone will not fit us for victory any more than it did for the sons of Sceva. The desire to dominate is no more noble than Goliath’s unbridled rage to destroy this young upstart. His adrenaline flowed as he scorned David’s youth, jumped to conclusions, was easily insulted, and marveled at the ignorance of others.

But David carried no such reactive mission. His endeavor was that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel. And all this assembly shall know that the LORD saveth not with sword and spear… –1 Samuel 17:47. Faithful action must be focused on yielding what you have, rather than obtaining what you don’t. If life erects concerns outside of our ability to change, it is fruitless to give them our attention. Joseph could not change his brothers’ reception, his master’s wife’s deception, the jail’s seclusion, or the butler’s delusion. The faith of the shepherd boy teaches us to stop lamenting over what we wanna-be and start being what we oughta-be. We need to stop looking for a miracle and start looking for an opportunity. It is not about overcoming extreme odds, but rather it is how we respond to a traffic jam, a disobedient child, an irate customer, or a demanding spouse. It is about owning a cause big enough to defuse selfish reaction and incite charitable pro-action.

Why would Japanese Kamikaze pilots die for a losing cause during World War Two? Why would Muslim terrorists blow themselves up? Why do Catholic Priests and Nuns take vows of celibacy and poverty? Is there no cause for the Christian that extends broader and deeper than the giants of this world? Is there not a cause that stirs our imagination and sanctifies our action? Or isn’t there even one that transforms our mundane work into a channel of grace for the service of the King of the Universe? How would history be different if Jesse would have spent his retirement like the elders of our day? God slays giants by the instruments we yield to him, from the needle of Dorcas… to the nail of Jael, from Zebedee’s boats of the business… to the boys of his bosom.

Shamgar had an oxgoad;
David had a sling;
Dorcus had a needle;
Rahab had a string;
Samson had a jawbone;
Moses had a rod;
Mary had some ointment;
And all were used for God!

E Davide disse: «Che cosa ho fatto ora? Non c’è forse una ragione?» –1 Samuele 17:29.

La storia di Davide e Golia ebbe luogo più di tre millenni fa e da allora è sempre stata una delle preferite di grandi e piccini. C’è qualcosa nella sorte del più debole che ci coinvolge tutti. Forse, inconsciamente, ci immaginiamo in circostanze simili e speriamo segretamente che un giorno anche la nostra «nave arrivi in porto» in modo altrettanto straordinario. Purtroppo, un successo così casuale sembra più adatto a una produzione hollywoodiana che alla vita reale. Vediamo soltanto il conflitto tra il giovane e l’anziano, il pastore e il guerriero, le pesanti armi militari e la fionda. Eppure, nella sua giovinezza, Davide abbracciò alcuni principi fondamentali che lo resero un candidato ideale al successo. Ma questi spesso passano inosservati, nel nostro amore per una vittoria romantica e culminante.

Se l’unica immagine che abbiamo di noi stessi proviene dallo specchio sociale che ci circonda, avremo una percezione interiore distorta, simile a quella che vediamo sbirciando in uno specchio deformante a una fiera. Le opinioni e le percezioni sociali del nostro ambiente spesso ci presentano, davanti agli occhi e alle orecchie, una descrizione goffa e distorta di chi siamo. A volte è irrealisticamente positiva e fa apparire una persona agli occhi dei media come un eroe, benché abbia dimostrato ben poco carattere eroico.

Il mondo dello sport è probabilmente il colpevole maggiore in questo senso. Si elogiano le persone che corrono, lanciano o tirano meglio di chiunque altro. Ma il talento sportivo aggiunge ben poco al loro valore intrinseco e autentico come esseri umani. L’altra faccia della medaglia produce una quantità enorme di messaggi negativi e umilianti, volti a scoraggiare ogni tentativo. Questi commenti piovono copiosi da genitori stressati, fratelli insicuri, capi frustrati e tanti altri conoscenti in cerca di un’identità in una società del «sopravvive il più forte». I messaggi provenienti da questi due schieramenti sono sconnessi e sproporzionati. Sentirsi dire che si è grandi non farà mai diventare grandi, così come una raffica di commenti denigratori non produrrà umiltà. Purtroppo, troppo spesso molti di noi permettono a queste proiezioni sproporzionate di influenzare il proprio pensiero e di tracciare il proprio cammino.

Il dono più grande e superiore concesso all’umanità rispetto al resto del creato non risiede nelle sue capacità fisiche, ma nella sua mente. Gli animali più intelligenti possono essere addestrati a essere responsabili, ma non possono scegliere né dirigere il proprio addestramento. Noi esseri umani, invece, possiamo scrivere per noi stessi nuovi programmi, del tutto indipendenti dai nostri istinti o dall’educazione ricevuta dal nostro ambiente. Chi vive in naturale accordo con i propri istinti e condizionamenti difficilmente si eleverà al di sopra del regno animale. Ma coloro che eserciteranno e svilupperanno questi doni potranno svolgere in modo unico il ruolo che Dio ha progettato per loro nel confronto con i giganti. Il tempo e la posizione di Davide erano unici, ma i principi che abbracciò erano universali. Se potessi insegnare al mio cane a cantare con lo jodel, dimostrerei che i cani possono farlo e aprirei la possibilità anche ad altri di riuscirci. Allo stesso modo, se Davide avesse sconfitto Golia soltanto per miracolo, non ci resterebbe alcuna speranza, se non sederci ad aspettare che Dio faccia lo stesso per noi. Se invece alla base della vittoria c’erano dei principi, abbiamo un esempio da seguire e una virtù da acquisire per metterla in pratica sul nostro campo di battaglia.

Quando quella mattina Davide si alzò di buon’ora e si mise sulle spalle il sacco di grano, pane e formaggio da portare ai fratelli, non aveva idea di cosa avrebbe portato la giornata. Il Signore era il suo pastore e nulla gli mancava, ma quando giunse sul posto rimase sconvolto da ciò che vide. I due eserciti erano schierati su montagne opposte e bloccati in una situazione di stallo. Scendere nella valle con tutto il proprio esercito per combattere contro il nemico in salita avrebbe comportato un enorme svantaggio. Nessuna delle due parti era disposta a correre un rischio simile. Così i Filistei proposero una modalità di combattimento comune, secondo cui due guerrieri si sarebbero affrontati nella valle, senza dare vantaggio a nessuna delle due parti. Ma tra i Filistei c’era un gigante che terrorizzava l’esercito d’Israele. Quando Davide chiese perché nessuno affrontasse le ingiurie blasfeme dell’infedele, si scontrò con il duro rimprovero del fratello maggiore: …l’ira di Eliab si accese contro Davide, e gli disse: «Perché sei sceso qui? E a chi hai lasciato quelle poche pecore nel deserto? Io conosco la tua superbia e la malvagità del tuo cuore; sei sceso per vedere la battaglia». Davide rispose: «Che cosa ho fatto ora? Non c’è forse una ragione?» –1 Samuele 17:28-29.

Fissando lo sguardo su Gesù, autore e perfezionatore della nostra fede; il quale, per la gioia che gli era posta dinanzi, sopportò la croce, disprezzando l’infamia, e si è seduto alla destra del trono di Dio –Ebrei 12:2. Quando un uomo ha davanti a sé una causa, può sopportare quasi qualsiasi cosa. Alcuni perseverano per una corona corruttibile. Il re Saul aveva promesso ricchezze esenti da tasse e il posto di genero, ma la ricompensa terrena non attirò alcun volontario. Sebbene l’idea di una posizione prestigiosa nel mondo non significasse nulla per il tenero cuore di Davide, le provocazioni blasfeme di Golia accesero in lui un fuoco di zelo, e Davide si fece avanti per fede. Ma la fede non è un semplice capriccio che si può gonfiare con una pompa emotiva. Infatti, come il corpo senza lo spirito è morto, così anche la fede senza le opere [l’azione] è morta –Giacomo 2:26. Così, con la causa ben chiara davanti a sé e il suo Dio al suo fianco, Davide si offrì di combattere contro Golia.

Così Davide andò avanti, agendo secondo principi pii e integri…

Una coscienza sollecita risiede nell’anima dell’uomo e determina ciò a cui teniamo. Molti pensano che la coscienza serva soltanto a porre dei limiti. Ma la coscienza umana è stata creata anche per svolgere la funzione opposta. Quando siamo convinti che qualcosa sia buono e giusto, lo perseguiamo con passione. Thomas Edison disse che il genio è l’1% ispirazione e il 99% sudore. Anche se può essere abbastanza vero, non c’è dubbio che l’ispirazione debba venire per prima. Le aspirazioni di Giacobbe per Rachele gli permisero di sopportare i sette anni di lavoro. La ricerca di Edison di una lampadina funzionante gli fece dimenticare le migliaia di elementi che non avevano funzionato.

L’apatia indifferente è l’opposto ed è il risultato di una coscienza cauterizzata. Davide era sbalordito che le provocazioni blasfeme di Golia non spingessero l’esercito di Dio ad agire. Date a un uomo una ragione per vivere e troverà il modo –Nietzke. Da prigioniero in un campo di concentramento nazista durante l’Olocausto, Victor Frankl fu assegnato al reparto del campo in cui i prigionieri morivano di tifo. Osservò che quando una persona perdeva la speranza, poco dopo sopraggiungeva la morte. Allo stesso modo, per molti dei nostri giorni, quando nella lotta svanisce la speranza di un guadagno personale, svanisce anche la passione di superare gli ostacoli. Oggi la maggior parte dei lavoratori è più interessata allo stipendio che a svolgere un lavoro valido e meritevole. Spesso, quando un uomo perde i sentimenti per la moglie, crede di non essere più capace di amarla; ma un uomo con una coscienza salda nei confronti dei principi divini agirà con amore verso di lei, indipendentemente dai propri sentimenti o dalla sua reazione. La coscienza risveglia e alimenta la causa, ponendo le basi per un’azione appassionata.

Un’immaginazione sincera appartiene alla sfera dello spirito ed è guidata dalla nostra coscienza. La necessità è la madre dell’invenzione –Sconosciuto. Alcuni aspettano che la vita si riveli, mentre altri la inventano strada facendo. Questo non è un permesso di sostenere ideali falsi. La ricerca di Davide è sincera, perché non era stato deformato dai media che lo circondavano. Sulle colline di Betlemme aveva avuto la meglio sulle bestie (un leone e un orso) e, con l’aiuto di Dio, non teme di affrontarne uno nella valle di Ela (un uomo che era guerriero fin dalla giovinezza).

Quando Saul acconsentì, seppur con riluttanza, alla proposta di Davide, procedette ad armare il ragazzo secondo il tipico stile mondano. Benché indossare l’armatura del re potesse essere un onore, Davide non ne volle sapere: …non posso andare con queste, perché non le ho mai provate. E Davide se le tolse –1 Samuele 17:39, scegliendo invece cinque pietre. Sapere cosa fanno gli altri e sapere cosa fare non sono necessariamente la stessa cosa.

Le convinzioni timorose dell’esercito israelita erano radicate in un sistema di valori pagano. Il problema non era Golia, bensì la paura priva di fede e la convinzione che si dovesse combattere alle condizioni imposte dal mondo. Chi abbraccia una causa autentica e meritevole troverà sicuramente l’immaginazione necessaria per perseguirla.

Golia aveva dato per scontato che avrebbe combattuto alle proprie condizioni. Offeso e adirato, gridò: …Vieni verso di me, e darò la tua carne agli uccelli del cielo e alle bestie dei campi –1 Samuele 17:44. Essendo un gigante, velocità e agilità non erano il suo forte, e perciò ordinò a Davide di andare da lui. Ma Golia aveva sopravvalutato enormemente le proprie capacità e sottovalutato il suo avversario. Secondo alcune stime, con sei o sette rotazioni al secondo, la fionda di Davide aveva una potenza d’arresto pari a quella di una pistola calibro .45, e la mano di un fromboliere esperto …poteva lanciare pietre a un capello di distanza senza mancare il bersaglio –Giudici 20:16. Non era raro che riuscissero a colpire gli uccelli in volo. Tra le rovine antiche sono state rinvenute delle pinze che si ritiene fossero usate dai militari per estrarre le pietre conficcate nei soldati feriti. Se Golia avesse avuto una lancia e Davide una pistola, non saremmo così pronti a credere che l’uomo più grande avesse il vantaggio principale.

L’azione fedele è inevitabile quando il nostro corpo è sottomesso alla nostra anima e al nostro spirito, e questi sono diretti dallo Spirito di Dio. Allora siamo liberi di agire indipendentemente dalla nostra natura e dalle altre influenze. Quando le passioni lussuriose del corpo mortale dominano il nostro cuore e la nostra mente, siamo sconfitti prima ancora di fare un passo verso il nemico. Come strumenti creati da Dio, dotati di libero arbitrio morale, abbiamo la capacità divina di scegliere come agire. Alcuni credono che essere proattivi significhi semplicemente prendere l’iniziativa. Ma l’iniziativa da sola non ci renderà idonei alla vittoria, così come non lo fece per i figli di Sceva. Il desiderio di dominare non è più nobile della furia incontrollata di Golia, deciso a distruggere quel giovane insolente. L’adrenalina gli scorreva in corpo mentre disprezzava la giovane età di Davide, saltava a conclusioni affrettate, si offendeva facilmente e si stupiva dell’ignoranza altrui.

Davide, però, non era guidato da una simile missione reattiva. Il suo intento era che tutta la terra sapesse che c’è un Dio in Israele. E tutta questa assemblea saprà che il SIGNORE non salva con la spada e con la lancia… –1 Samuele 17:47. L’azione fedele deve concentrarsi sul mettere a disposizione ciò che si ha, anziché ottenere ciò che non si ha. Se la vita fa sorgere preoccupazioni che non siamo in grado di cambiare, è inutile dedicarvi la nostra attenzione. Giuseppe non poteva cambiare l’accoglienza dei suoi fratelli, l’inganno della moglie del suo padrone, l’isolamento della prigione o l’illusione del coppiere. La fede del giovane pastore ci insegna a smettere di lamentarci di ciò che vorremmo essere e a cominciare a essere ciò che dovremmo essere. Dobbiamo smettere di cercare un miracolo e cominciare a cercare un’opportunità. Non si tratta di superare avversità estreme, ma di come reagiamo a un ingorgo, a un figlio disubbidiente, a un cliente furioso o a un coniuge esigente. Si tratta di abbracciare una causa abbastanza grande da disinnescare le reazioni egoistiche e suscitare azioni proattive e generose.

Perché i piloti giapponesi kamikaze morirono per una causa destinata alla sconfitta durante la Seconda guerra mondiale? Perché i terroristi musulmani si fanno esplodere? Perché i sacerdoti e le suore cattolici fanno voto di celibato e povertà? Non c’è forse per il cristiano una causa più ampia e profonda dei giganti di questo mondo? Non c’è forse una causa che risveglia la nostra immaginazione e santifica le nostre azioni? O non ce n’è almeno una che trasformi il nostro lavoro quotidiano in un canale di grazia al servizio del Re dell’Universo? Quanto sarebbe stata diversa la storia se Iesse avesse trascorso la pensione come gli anziani dei nostri giorni? Dio abbatte i giganti mediante gli strumenti che gli mettiamo a disposizione: dall’ago di Dorkas… al chiodo di Iael, dalle barche dell’attività di Zebedeo… ai ragazzi stretti al suo cuore.

Samgar aveva un pungolo per buoi;
Davide aveva una fionda;
Dorkas aveva un ago;
Rahab aveva una corda;
Sansone aveva una mascella d’asino;
Mosè aveva un bastone;
Maria aveva dell’unguento;
E tutti furono usati da Dio!

One day you may be walking along a seashore. You glance back to watch your footprints disappear with the next surge of foaming water. You love to hear the soothing swish of the breakers. You gaze at the graceful sweep of shoreline and glittering ocean way out to the horizon. Life is good.

Suddenly a huge wave sweeps in and lifts you off your feet. You struggle and flail to regain your footing. Or the wave may even carry you farther and slam you against a rock wall, leaving you stunned and gasping in pain.

This wave may be called grief, as expressed in the following stanza from the song by Mary A. Baker.

Master, with anguish of spirit
I bow in my grief today;
The depths of my sad heart are troubled;
Oh, waken and save, I pray!
Torrents of sin and of anguish
Sweep o’er my sinking soul!
And I perish! I perish, dear Master;
Oh hasten, and take control.

In the past year, many of us have lost loved ones. Perhaps it was a childhood friend, or someone from our church family, or even from our immediate family. Depending on how close we were, we felt drops, splashes, or even tidal waves of grief.

Our grief stems from the relationship we shared. We have invested in each other’s lives to some degree. We have loved, but now that love has nowhere to go. We could say that grief is the price of love.

Here is how one widow described grief: “At the sudden and untimely death of my husband, the feeling was one of overwhelming shock, disbelief, and even panic, as I faced an uncertain future without him at the age of 51. Looking back, I realize how merciful God is to allow us to be in a certain state of numbness and shock at a time like this, allowing the reality to sink in more slowly.”

How did she cope? She says, “I am also awed at how He provides the grace and strength to go through hard things in life that we never thought we would have to face. He walks with us as we go through the valley of grief, so we are never walking alone. The journey of grief is not the same for everyone. It is not over in a few months. For me, I still cried a year later. It took a long time for the pain to fade and for life to become meaningful again. But praise God, that time does come! It is best not to look too far into the future. We walk one day at a time with Jesus, knowing that the best is yet to come.”

Here are more experiences from those who have been there:

  • “I am still learning that when we say, ‘It’s all right, Lord,’ we need to leave it there, at Jesus’ feet.”
  • “Grieving people are very lonely, but there’s also an aloneness that comes from not having a place to belong. You may be in a room of people, and still feel utterly alone, because you’ve lost your sense of belonging, or your category of belonging has changed.”
  • “The presence of a grieving person can be painful for others. It’s a reminder that “bad” things can happen. So, at times they are not invited, which is painful. A grieving person wants to be invited, but at times when included they feel their lack of belonging anew and think they should have stayed at home. Most times, casual conversation can be difficult for them when their world has been violently shaken. Their hearts are heavy while the mood of others is lighthearted, making them feel even more despondent. Understandably, many people don’t know what to do when they see others grieving, so they default to doing nothing and walk away. Many friendships are lost after a loss, which is even more painful.”
  • “God was so close. He was always there. ‘Underneath are the everlasting arms’, and I felt them.”

God can use sorrow and grief to teach us what we might not learn in happier times. We learn to depend on Him. We think of the seriousness of life. We learn to embrace eternal values and anticipate heaven. We are motivated to cherish the loved ones we still have when we hear expressions such as this: “Looking back, I wish we would not have taken the time we had together for granted. I wish I would have recognized his personality traits as strengths rather than things that annoyed.”

Those who lose loved ones often find themselves in the limelight for a time. Many people want to know how they are responding, especially when the death is an unusual situation. Consider the experience of Elizabeth Elliot and the four others who were made widows in 1956 by jungle killers in Ecuador. Or think of Marie Troyer whose husband John was murdered by guerrillas in Guatemala in 1981, or the mothers of the girls killed in Nickel Mines, Pennsylvania in 2006.

These women found themselves in the glare of an almost worldwide spotlight. Their greatest opportunity to display God’s enabling grace likely came at a time when they wanted it least. But their responses of forgiveness, unselfishness, and trust in God amazed the world, at least considering the amount of media attention. Truly, A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid –Matthew 5:14.

While we and those we know will hardly face that level of exposure, we too have a unique platform to display God’s grace. We may never have a better opportunity to touch hardened or seeking hearts than in our own hour of grief.

When we hear that people have indeed been drawn to God through the death of our loved one, it can be a source of comfort and meaning. This death was not a senseless tragedy; it was meant to bring glory to God. In other words, God does not waste our sorrows.

It reminds us of Jesus’ words about Lazarus when he said, …This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God might be glorified thereby –John 11:4. Jesus is our perfect example for relating to those in sorrow. He came to Mary and Martha and listened. He cried with them even though He knew He could and then did transform the whole situation by raising Lazarus.

How do we help?

What is our part in helping a grieving sister glorify God in the midst of her situation? Consider the thoughts shared by the following widows:

  • “What helped was when a dear sister sat with me and told me she cared. And in her quietness, I could feel that her love was real.”
  • “Grief is surprising and unexpected. The person may be having a good day when they hear a song, smell a certain scent, or see a familiar article of clothing which triggers a memory followed by a flood of tears. If this happens when you’re with them, it’s okay. Tears are okay. Tears are healing. Stay present and help them through it. Press in; grieve with them. It’s better to err in doing something than in doing nothing. You may not understand. That’s okay. You don’t need to experience loss to show that you care.”
  • “Grief is exhausting and mentally debilitating. So don’t just ask what you can do; look for a need they may have and try to fill it. For example, ‘I’d like to come over Tuesday evening and fix your faucet’ or ‘We’d like to come and bring a meal if you’re up to it?’”
  • “One thing that meant a lot to me was when people shared pleasant memories of our loved one, or things they appreciated about him. Even today, almost nineteen years later, it still warms my heart when people do that.”
  • “It was all the cards that came every day for the first two months after my husband died. I looked forward to them every day, and the first day without a card was hard.”
  • “What really helped me was when someone told me to focus on my blessings; that they are praying for me, and they care. Or they invited me to go along even if the number was then lopsided. Another thing was when they stopped by for coffee breaks or when they sent a text.”
  • “Widows need encouragement on their anniversary date and on the date their husband died. It means a lot if someone ‘actually’ remembers! A widow’s supper is nice. So is having a secret sister. It helped when someone gave a listening ear and was there to help with the work and the young children. Most of all, I knew people were praying for us.”

What do we say?

We may struggle with what to say to a bereaved friend. After all, we do not want to be like Job’s wife or his friends whose words only increased Job’s suffering. Here are some perspectives:

  • “They need not tell us we are alone now. We know that already.”
  • “Grief may really shake someone’s faith in God, momentarily paralyzing them, especially if they haven’t experienced much trauma before. As much as they long to trust God and accept this new reality in their lives, sometimes it takes time to simply get through the shock and be able to talk to God again. This is okay. They will most likely find healing and deepen their faith, but give them space to struggle, wrestle, and grieve deeply. Listen and try to refrain from “fixing” their faith with words such as “All things work together for good…”, or “At least you…”
  • “Asking a grieving person how they are doing could put them in a difficult position. Asking in a crowd of people may not be the best time. It may be best not to ask unless you really want to know and are willing to take the time to listen.”
  • “It is hard to think rationally in those first hard months. I did not appreciate being asked those first months what I would do for a living. I first needed to process my grief. I was also trying to help my young daughters who were devastated at the loss of their beloved daddy. That decision could wait.”

The following excerpts reveal other struggles with grief:

  • “Everyone grieves differently; there is no right or wrong way. And it never goes away even though all my friends’ lives go on as normal, which is very painful to watch. Holidays are very hard. Attending weddings is almost not doable. This is a couple’s world and only by the grace of God is it possible. Actually, the weeks before the annual anniversary dates are harder than the actual days.”
  • “One thing I realized very quickly was that we live in a very couple-orientated world. At the loss of a spouse, one is left trying to figure out where they fit in. I deeply appreciate, when I’m in a group setting that includes widows and singles, that there are those who try to make me feel included and not the odd one out.”
  • “You can’t put a time limit on grief. It’s different for everyone. There’s no ‘getting over it’ so that it doesn’t hurt anymore. If grieved properly, the wound is not as raw, and it becomes a scar. It’s like getting used to living without an arm or a leg. You adjust to it not being there, but you never stop missing it.”
  • “Death in the family or losing a spouse is harder than one can imagine until they are going through the same thing. I wish we would have had more church support. Our boys need a father figure to follow, one to teach them what a dad would.”
  • “Our children make mistakes as other children do; they need encouragement, not criticism. Also, they could use a helping hand with their work. I wish I would not have needed to leave my youngest child alone so much when I went to work. I broke out in a sweat more than once wondering where the money was coming from to pay the bills, but I thank the Lord that it was always there.”

How can we remember to support the grieving beyond those first days and weeks? We could mark our calendars with the dates of their birthdays, anniversaries, and their loved one’s death date. Then we could designate a certain day of the week to do something for them. If we make a plan, we are more likely to carry out our good intentions.

Finally, we should also remember the “widows who aren’t”. Sometimes there are those among us whose life is racked by a grief worse than that of an actual death. Perhaps there was betrayal, abandonment, incarceration, or suicide in their life’s journey. They may almost envy the clean wound of the “normal” widow. Or they may struggle with guilt on top of their grief.

These situations are often located far outside our comfort zones. There are no easy answers of how to deal with them. But let us not stay aloof from such a sister if we have the opportunity. God will help us find a way to show we care if we ask Him.

As we, and those we love, keep walking with God, may we portray the scene in the final verse of the song mentioned earlier:

“Master, the terror is over, the elements sweetly rest;
Earth’s sun in the calm lake is mirrored,
And heaven’s within my breast.
Linger, O blessed Redeemer,
Leave me alone no more;
And with joy I shall make the blest harbor,
And rest on the blissful shore.”

Let’s conclude with a quote from a widow:

“Walk with them until they can come out of the cave and feel the sunshine again. It may require hard work and getting messy at times, but to them you will be Jesus ‘with skin on’. You are not responsible for their healing; only Jesus can do that. But you can bring them to Him.

Remember the friends that brought the paralyzed man to Jesus, lowering him through the roof. And, behold, they brought to him a man sick of the palsy, lying on a bed: and Jesus seeing their faith said unto the sick of the palsy; Son, be of good cheer; thy sins be forgiven thee … And Jesus knowing their thoughts said, Wherefore think ye evil in your hearts? For whether is easier, to say, Thy sins be forgiven thee; or to say, Arise, and walk? But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power on earth to forgive sins, (then saith he to the sick of the palsy,) Arise, take up thy bed, and go unto thine house. And he arose, and departed to his house. But when the multitudes saw it, they marvelled, and glorified God, which had given such power unto men –Matthew 9:2-8.

What a beautiful picture! In like manner, you can carry your grief-‘paralyzed’ friend to Jesus. Watch them be healed, shoulder their burden of grief, and then move on toward their heavenly home. As we see God doing a work in their heart, we can all praise God together!”

~In this article, the sections in quotation marks were shared with the author by a number of anonymous widows.
